provenance.edition_identity: William Doyle, The Oxford History of the French Revolution, 2002 edition; IndexerLabs-derived PDF missing front matter and endnotes

page_review.word_count_method: Words extracted from owned document pages 86-111 after removing page numbers, running heads, the chapter number and display title, and superscript note markers; substantive body text and block quotations retained.

excluded_regions.role: chapter number and display title excluded from indexable word count; chapter identity retained as structural metadata
superscript note markers excluded from word count; note text unavailable

unavailable_regions.reason: Absent from the supplied special edition. Superscript note markers remain in body text, but the note text is unavailable and excluded from discovery.

visual_review.finding: All owned and context pages were legible text pages with no maps, tables, captions, or image-only regions requiring separate treatment.

selection_method.unit: independently searchable source subject rather than proposed index heading
principles: Retain principal subjects and significant localized or subsidiary subjects even when confined to one passage.
Split subjects when a reader could plausibly seek one without the other or when a combined label would overstate page support.
Retain named people, institutions, works, places, and events only when the chapter analyzes them, uses them as sustained explanatory cases, or makes them independently useful to scholarly readers.
Preserve causal qualification, chronological distinction, and the author's stated uncertainty.
Use optional only for defensible supplemental access whose absence would not materially reduce usefulness.
Do not use density calibration to set subject count or priority.
selection_method.fresh_source_led_pass: The frozen source pages and policy were reviewed and the full subject inventory was drafted before any earlier chapter discovery artifact was consulted. Earlier discoveries were then consulted only for field naming and procedural consistency.

reader_task_catalog.question: Explain how weather, harvests, bread prices, unemployment, and trade policy conditioned the political crisis.
Distinguish the 1614 order-based model from the Dauphine/Vizille model and explain why doubling without vote by head left the conflict unresolved.
Trace how press freedom, clubs, pamphlets, petitions, and provincial conflicts converted anti-despotism into anti-privilege mobilization.
Explain the Result of the Council and why it satisfied one representation demand while postponing the decisive voting question.
Describe the 1789 electoral system, its democratic reach, its social filters, and its effects on representation.
Compare the elected clergy, nobility, and third estate, including their social composition, internal divisions, and deeper solidarities.
Trace verification of powers from procedural dispute to a unilateral claim of national legitimacy.
Explain the roles of Sieyes, Mirabeau, political journalism, public galleries, and the Palais Royal in creating the National Assembly.
Compare the Tennis Court Oath and the Royal Session as rival constitutional and sovereign claims.
Explain why royal enforcement failed and why clergy and nobles united with the National Assembly on 27 June.
Connect troop movements, Necker's dismissal, bread scarcity, militia formation, French Guards' defection, and the Bastille.
Explain why troop withdrawal marked the end of enforceable royal authority and why July constituted Revolution rather than ordinary revolt.

subjects.label: Economic crisis of 1788-1789
subjects.meaning: Interlocking harvest, price, employment, and consumption shocks formed the material setting in which constitutional conflict became volatile.
subjects.stance: The chapter treats economic distress as a powerful condition and accelerator of political change, not as a sufficient single-cause explanation.

target_labels: Popular intervention in the constitutional revolution

evidence.evidence_summary: The chapter opens by connecting nationwide harvest disruption and extreme winter conditions to rapidly rising grain prices.
Falling consumption and industrial layoffs deepen hardship and make the old political order widely blameworthy.
The electoral season unfolds amid rising bread prices, unemployment, and repeated market disorder.
The July confrontation occurs when troop anxiety and political suspicion coincide with severe food shortages.
The chapter's conclusion links the political breakdown to a popular movement powerful enough to defeat royal coercion.

subjects.label: Catastrophic weather and harvest failures
subjects.meaning: Hail, drought, and the exceptionally severe winter of 1788-1789 damaged crops and transport across much of France.
subjects.stance: Weather is presented as a nationwide material shock that worsened an already unstable economy.

evidence.evidence_summary: A destructive July hailstorm, preceding drought, and a long winter damaged grain, vines, and olives across regions.
Frozen transport and workplaces prolonged the human and industrial effects of the winter.

subjects.label: Grain-market policy and deregulation
subjects.meaning: Removal of grain controls under Calonne and their restoration under Necker shaped supply, prices, and public expectations.
subjects.stance: The author distinguishes policy effects from weather and notes that later deputies' preference for free trade collided with immediate subsistence politics.

target_labels: Grain-trade debate in the National Assembly

evidence.evidence_summary: The text explains that the removal of controls dissipated earlier surpluses before Necker restored regulation too late to stop price increases.
Free grain trade joined the commercial treaty as a government policy blamed by working people.
The Assembly debates grain freedom inconclusively because doctrinal preference conflicts with the political danger of scarcity.

subjects.label: Bread prices and subsistence burden
subjects.meaning: Escalating grain, flour, and bread prices absorbed extraordinary shares of working people's income and repeatedly generated fear and disorder.
subjects.stance: The chapter makes subsistence pressure a continuing bridge between economic distress, public mobilization, and the July uprising.

target_labels: Storming and surrender of the Bastille

evidence.evidence_summary: Bread could consume most of a poor worker's earnings as grain prices climbed through the winter and spring.
Restored magistrates recognize that rising bread prices could push public celebration beyond control.
Electoral excitement is accompanied by price fixing, searches for hoarded grain, and growing unemployment.
Paris bread prices approach a twenty-year high as Necker's dismissal turns political fear into armed mobilization.
The search for arms and food insecurity converge in the movement toward the Bastille.

subjects.label: Industrial depression and unemployment
subjects.meaning: Falling consumer demand, textile contraction, and widespread layoffs magnified hardship in towns and countryside.
subjects.stance: The author presents industrial decline as real but multi-causal, resisting claims that one technology or treaty alone caused it.

evidence.evidence_summary: Collapsing demand reduced output sharply and left large numbers of textile workers without employment.
The continuing industrial crisis swells unemployment during the election campaign.

subjects.label: Machinery-breaking and technological resentment
subjects.meaning: Workers attacked spinning machinery they believed displaced higher-cost traditional labor.
subjects.stance: The passage treats machinery as a target of blame within a broader depression, not as its sole proven cause.

evidence.evidence_summary: Rouen workers destroy spinning machines and workshops amid fears that new methods undercut traditional production.

subjects.label: Anglo-French commercial treaty of 1786
subjects.meaning: The commercial agreement opened France to cheaper British manufactured imports and aggravated industrial weakness.
subjects.stance: The author explicitly qualifies popular attribution: the treaty worsened the depression but had not operated long enough to explain all claimed damage.

target_labels: Popular blame of government for economic distress

evidence.evidence_summary: British imports are judged to have intensified an existing slump, although public blame exceeded what the treaty's short operation could support.

subjects.label: Popular blame of government for economic distress
subjects.meaning: Working people associated grain policy, commercial policy, scarcity, and unemployment with governmental failure.
subjects.stance: The chapter treats these perceptions as politically consequential even where the causal attribution was overstated.

target_labels: Popular intervention in the constitutional revolution

evidence.evidence_summary: Grain deregulation and the British treaty give workers concrete reasons to blame the government for worsening conditions.
Rumors and suspected hoarding turn electoral agitation toward established authorities and property.
Necker's association with controlled grain supply makes his dismissal inseparable from fear of starvation and military action.

subjects.label: Necker's return, popularity, and political role
subjects.meaning: Necker combined extraordinary public credit with cautious, popularity-conscious policies that opened debate, shaped representation, and postponed decisive constitutional choices.
subjects.stance: The author neither treats Necker as an architect of revolution nor dismisses his influence: his equivocation repeatedly left conflicts for others to resolve, while his public standing made his dismissal explosive.

target_labels: Result of the King's Council of State, 27 December 1788

evidence.evidence_summary: On returning to office Necker restores grain controls after price increases are already under way.
His return produces public jubilation while the restoration policy also releases volatile street mobilization.
He relaxes press controls and reconvenes the Notables rather than deciding the Estates' form directly.
He concedes doubled third-estate numbers but leaves common voting to future voluntary agreement.
His electoral design shapes the social composition of deputies despite little direct interference.
At the opening he equivocates on common voting and leaves verification to separate orders.
He favors conciliation and a reforming Royal Session but loses control of the Court's revisions.
His July dismissal by the Court party immediately destabilizes an already frightened capital.

subjects.label: Restoration and decline of the parlements
subjects.meaning: The restored courts briefly embodied victory over despotism but lost public authority when they appeared to defend order privilege.
subjects.stance: The chapter emphasizes the speed with which institutional heroes became suspect once the representation question displaced the anti-despotic consensus.

evidence.evidence_summary: Necker's restoration of the courts produces popular celebration mixed with attacks and bloodshed.
The Paris court invokes the 1614 precedent to prevent a docile assembly, unintentionally aligning itself with unequal representation.
Magistrates formerly treated as national heroes become objects of hostility when the public rejects the precedent.
A narrow parliamentary retreat fails to restore credibility because it does not endorse third-estate claims.

subjects.label: Paris disorder after Necker's return
subjects.meaning: Street celebration of political restoration repeatedly crossed into attacks on authority and lethal confrontation.
subjects.stance: The episode is treated as early evidence that elite political victories had unleashed a public force no authority fully controlled.

target_labels: Popular intervention in the constitutional revolution
Public order and collapse of coercive authority
Restoration and decline of the parlements

evidence.evidence_summary: Celebrations include attacks on guard posts and officials' homes, followed by troop fire and casualties.
Renewed demonstrations accompany the Paris parlement's return, prompting an inquiry and warnings about loss of control.

subjects.label: Estates-General forms of 1614
subjects.meaning: The last precedent prescribed separate, nearly equal order chambers and voting by order.
subjects.stance: The source treats this precedent as constitutionally intelligible but politically retrograde and grossly unequal in 1788.

target_labels: Vote by head versus vote by order

evidence.evidence_summary: The Paris parlement specifies 1614 forms, revealing separate order chambers in which clergy and nobility could always outvote the third.
The Vizille settlement makes the older structure appear anachronistic to reformers.
Opposition to 1614 becomes a national anti-privilege campaign.
Notables largely defend the traditional structure, reinforcing their privileged image.

subjects.label: Representation of the three orders
subjects.meaning: Clergy, nobility, and third estate were both social orders and competing constitutional bodies whose separate or common representation determined national legitimacy.
subjects.stance: The chapter shows that numerical representation, verification, deliberation, and voting could not be separated from the orders' conflicting claims.

target_labels: Union of the three orders, 27 June 1789

evidence.evidence_summary: The 1614 precedent assigns separate elected chambers and order voting.
Electoral regulations create distinct order assemblies and a two-two-four deputy ratio.
Separate verification becomes the practical test of whether the orders will remain distinct.
Clerical defections make the third's claim broader than a single order.
The king finally orders remaining clergy and nobles into the National Assembly.

subjects.label: Doubling the third estate
subjects.meaning: Reformers demanded that third-estate deputies equal the combined numbers of clergy and nobility.
subjects.stance: The concession was politically decisive but structurally incomplete because vote by order could still nullify the numerical gain.

target_labels: Vote by head versus vote by order
Result of the King's Council of State, 27 December 1788

evidence.evidence_summary: Vizille establishes double third-estate representation together with election and head voting as an integrated model.
A nationwide consensus for doubling and vote by head emerges through organized agitation.
The Notables reject doubling despite overwhelming public pressure.
Necker grants doubled numbers but withholds a decision on common voting.
National electoral rules implement four third-estate deputies for every two from each privileged order.

subjects.label: Vote by head versus vote by order
subjects.meaning: Whether deputies voted individually or as three corporate orders determined whether the doubled third could exercise political power.
subjects.stance: The author identifies this unresolved rule as the core issue that moved the conflict from representation to verification and sovereignty.

target_labels: Result of the King's Council of State, 27 December 1788

evidence.evidence_summary: Vote by order under the 1614 precedent guarantees combined privileged control.
The Dauphine model couples doubled numbers with individual voting.
The December settlement declines to impose head voting and leaves deputies to confront the issue.
Noble cahiers show division between order voting, compromise, and a small pro-head minority.
The third treats common verification as necessary to prevent separate voting.
Failure of agreement leads the Commons to verify unilaterally and cross the legal threshold.

subjects.label: Dauphine and the Vizille principles
subjects.meaning: Dauphine's assemblies developed elected representation, double third-estate numbers, and vote by head as a coherent alternative to 1614.
subjects.stance: The province is presented as both a constitutional model and a training ground for experienced patriot leaders.

target_labels: Vote by head versus vote by order

evidence.evidence_summary: Vizille and Romans combine elected deputies, double third representation, and head voting into a model for national reform.
Other provinces expose how difficult it is to reproduce Dauphine's settlement where entrenched representation differs.
The national electoral rules preserve Dauphine's exceptional provincial route.
Dauphine deputies use their prior political experience to oppose separate verification.

subjects.label: Revival and reform of provincial estates
subjects.meaning: Efforts to revive provincial representative bodies became a test of whether entrenched order privileges could be reformed.
subjects.stance: The chapter shows that provincial estates supplied models and conflicts but were ultimately separated from most national elections.

evidence.evidence_summary: Dauphine's restored estates prompt other provinces to demand similar representative reform.
Existing provincial rules make equal representation politically and practically difficult, especially in Brittany.
Privileged participants in several provinces resist both internal inclusion and third-estate claims.
January regulations end most expectations that provincial estates will elect national deputies.

subjects.label: Press freedom under Necker
subjects.meaning: Necker released imprisoned journalists and declined to enforce traditional press controls.
subjects.stance: He expected open debate to enlarge ministerial freedom, but publicity instead accelerated mobilization beyond governmental control.

evidence.evidence_summary: Relaxed controls unleash public debate over national representation.
Political societies exploit the freer environment to commission and distribute anti-privilege pamphlets.
The agitation becomes self-reinforcing and exceeds the control of its elite organizers.

subjects.label: Political clubs and discussion societies
subjects.meaning: Parisian and provincial associations coordinated debate, pamphlets, petitions, and emerging leadership.
subjects.stance: The source treats them as catalytic networks rather than sovereign directors of a movement that soon escaped their control.

evidence.evidence_summary: Revived club life produces an elite Paris network opposed to the 1614 forms.
Local circles help respectable townspeople coordinate meetings and petitions.
Once mobilization spreads, commoner leaders and lawyers increasingly act independently of aristocratic sponsors.

subjects.label: Society of Thirty
subjects.meaning: Duport's largely noble reform society organized publicity against 1614 and privilege and promoted double representation and head voting.
subjects.stance: The author credits it with focusing national agitation while emphasizing that it deliberately inflamed bourgeois anxieties and quickly lost control of the movement.

target_labels: Bourgeois political awakening and anti-privilege mobilization
Sieyes and What Is the Third Estate?

evidence.evidence_summary: The society brings nobles, magistrates, writers, and public figures together to finance anti-privilege propaganda and model petitions.
Its campaign helps create a nationwide petition movement that soon becomes autonomous.
The largely non-third-estate sponsorship cannot prevent widening hostility from driving reform nobles into a minority.
Commoner organizers emerge and the campaign passes beyond metropolitan aristocratic direction.

subjects.label: Pamphleteering and political publicity
subjects.meaning: An extraordinary flow of pamphlets, periodicals, petitions, and rapid reports defined the terms of representation and privilege for a mass political audience.
subjects.stance: The chapter treats publicity as an active causal force that polarized positions, supplied constitutional language, and constrained deputies.

target_labels: Third estate as nation and semantic shift in patriotism
Spectators, crowds, and public pressure at Versailles

evidence.evidence_summary: With censorship relaxed, the representation debate expands rapidly through Paris publishing.
Commissioned pamphlets and circulated petitions cast 1614 as a privileged conspiracy.
Sieyes's tract gives the most forceful national formulation within a much larger anti-privilege print wave.
Model grievance texts circulate during elections and influence local cahiers.
Daily newspaper reports connect the verification stalemate to a wider aroused public.
Palais-Royal publication and oratory sustain pressure during the Assembly's decisive turn.

subjects.label: National petition movement
subjects.meaning: Coordinated town meetings and hundreds of petitions pressed the crown for equitable third-estate representation.
subjects.stance: The movement is presented as a national escalation that began with elite models but became locally driven and self-accelerating.

evidence.evidence_summary: Model petitions give municipalities a template for demanding doubled representation and head voting.
Local meetings and circles generate more than eight hundred petitions by year's end.
Provincial conflicts produce additional petitions from excluded or underrepresented groups.

subjects.label: Second Assembly of Notables
subjects.meaning: The reconvened, overwhelmingly noble body rejected doubling and declined to endorse vote by head.
subjects.stance: Its proceedings are treated as politically counterproductive: they delayed the Estates-General and confirmed the image of a privileged mouthpiece despite support for fiscal equality.

target_labels: Result of the King's Council of State, 27 December 1788

evidence.evidence_summary: Most Notables reject doubled third-estate representation and refuse to decide head voting amid intense public agitation.
Resistance by princes and privileged bodies reinforces suspicion after the Assembly disperses.
Necker's December decision rejects the Notables on doubling but follows them by withholding common voting.

subjects.label: Princes of the blood and defense of privilege
subjects.meaning: Most princes petitioned against doubling and head voting, connecting concession to threats against property and noble survival.
subjects.stance: The episode matters as a crystallization of privileged fears, not as proof that all nobles shared one position.

target_labels: Privilege as a political and social concept

evidence.evidence_summary: Five princes warn that representation reform would expose property and nobility to broader attack; the king rejects their advice.

subjects.label: Result of the King's Council of State, 27 December 1788
subjects.meaning: The royal decision doubled third-estate representation and opened cross-order election while refusing to impose vote by head.
subjects.stance: The author presents it as a popular triumph purchased by deferring the fundamental voting question into the Estates themselves.
acceptable_access: King's Council decision on the Estates-General

target_labels: Vote by head versus vote by order

evidence.evidence_summary: Necker rejects the Notables by doubling the third and allowing cross-order election, but leaves common voting to voluntary agreement.
The decision closes the first electoral phase while intensifying order polarization and third-estate mobilization.
January regulations translate the numerical concession into a two-two-four deputy allocation.

subjects.label: Constitutional conflict becoming social conflict
subjects.meaning: The earlier consensus against despotism broke apart when representation was recast as a struggle between the productive nation and privileged orders.
subjects.stance: The chapter explicitly marks this repolarization as rapid, mutually reinforcing, and central to the failure of compromise.

target_labels: Bourgeois political awakening and anti-privilege mobilization
Privilege as a political and social concept

evidence.evidence_summary: Debate over 1614 converts former parliamentary heroes into suspected defenders of social subjection.
The author states that constitutional questions recede as social divisions destroy the earlier anti-despotic consensus.
Bourgeois resentment and privileged defensiveness amplify each other, leaving reformers within privileged orders isolated.
Brittany demonstrates the conflict turning physically violent.

subjects.label: Bourgeois political awakening and anti-privilege mobilization
subjects.meaning: Educated commoners recognized a durable public role and organized to make the third estate politically dominant.
subjects.stance: The author treats bourgeois mobilization as politically transformative while distinguishing its leaders from poorer urban and rural populations.

target_labels: Third estate as nation and semantic shift in patriotism

evidence.evidence_summary: Elite reformers deliberately appeal to middle-class resentments to build national pressure.
Respectable townspeople organize meetings and petitions through local associations.
The bourgeoisie moves from spectatorship toward an expected dominant role in public life.
Commoner leaders, especially lawyers, take command of petitions, pamphlets, and local organization.

subjects.label: Privilege as a political and social concept
subjects.meaning: Privilege moved from a defended corporate right and fiscal exception to a general indictment of unequal law and political exclusion.
subjects.stance: The source preserves competing meanings: defenders linked privilege to property and order, while anti-privilege writers made its incompatibility with national common law decisive.

target_labels: Third estate as nation and semantic shift in patriotism

evidence.evidence_summary: The Society of Thirty's campaign casts privileges as socially divisive obstacles to national public spirit.
Princes defend privilege by presenting reform as a threat to property and nobility.
Sieyes defines privilege as exception to common law and excludes privileged groups from the properly constituted nation.
Noble delegates show broad willingness to surrender fiscal privilege but no comparable agreement on political forms.
The Royal Session preserves feudal property and order vetoes even while offering fiscal and administrative reform.

subjects.label: Sieyes and What Is the Third Estate?
subjects.meaning: Sieyes supplied the most forceful argument that the third estate constituted the nation and that privileged orders lacked a legitimate place within common law.
subjects.stance: The author treats his formulations as both highly influential and strategically radical, while noting that some earlier privilege claims were overstated.

target_labels: Third estate as nation and semantic shift in patriotism
Sieyes's final appeal and roll-call, 10-12 June
Declaration of the National Assembly, 17 June

evidence.evidence_summary: An early Sieyes pamphlet attacks privilege, though it misleadingly suggests a noble and clerical monopoly.
What Is the Third Estate? defines the nation through common law, identifies the third with the whole, and recommends unilateral national assembly.
Sieyes moves the final appeal and unilateral verification that begin the legal rupture.
He steers the naming debate toward a National Assembly representing the French nation.
The adopted title and tax resolution realize the sovereign implications of his reasoning.

subjects.label: Third estate as nation and semantic shift in patriotism
subjects.meaning: Third-estate claims increasingly appropriated the language of nation and patriotism, displacing its earlier focus on resistance to despotism.
subjects.stance: The chapter presents this semantic change as both a source of unity for commoners and an exclusionary pressure on compromise.

target_labels: Sieyes and What Is the Third Estate?
The third estate's adoption of 'the Commons'
Declaration of the National Assembly, 17 June

evidence.evidence_summary: The author marks the breakdown of anti-despotic consensus as third-estate social claims become dominant.
Nation and patriotism are redefined around the third estate and opposition to privilege.
Deputies call themselves the Commons, signaling a representative claim beyond one order.
Common verification and clerical defections force a decision about speaking for the French nation.
Adoption of the National Assembly title converts the semantic claim into institutional sovereignty.

subjects.label: Brittany provincial-estates crisis
subjects.meaning: Breton conflict over representation, privilege, and provincial procedure produced deadlock, violence, and later electoral exceptions.
subjects.stance: The chapter treats Brittany as a sustained demonstration that provincial constitutional forms could intensify rather than resolve order conflict.

target_labels: Revival and reform of provincial estates

evidence.evidence_summary: Town demands in Rennes and Nantes challenge noble and clerical representation before the scheduled estates meeting.
Third-estate refusal and noble noncompliance suspend proceedings and destroy prospects of reconciliation.
Popular demonstrations and armed clashes end with the nobility besieged and political compromise broken.
Because provincial conflict prevented an estate-based election, Breton orders receive exceptional national procedures.
The nobility boycotts the national elections and sends no delegates.

subjects.label: Emergence of third-estate political leaders
subjects.meaning: Pamphleteers, petition organizers, municipal activists, and experienced professionals developed recognized leadership after elite reformers launched the campaign.
subjects.stance: The author emphasizes that commoner leadership emerged through practice and soon acted independently of aristocratic sponsorship.

evidence.evidence_summary: Commoner writers and town organizers begin articulating grievances and coordinating provincial action in their own names.
Professional conflicts give advocates and petty judges motives and forums for sustained political engagement.
Well-known leaders join a much larger contingent of locally experienced but nationally untested deputies.

subjects.label: Lawyers in revolutionary political mobilization
subjects.meaning: Advocates, judges, notaries, and officeholders supplied the procedural skills, institutional experience, and grievances that made them leading organizers and deputies.
subjects.stance: The chapter treats legal dominance as structurally produced and politically consequential, while not equating lawyers with the whole third estate.

target_labels: Revolutionary legality and the law-soaked third estate

evidence.evidence_summary: Lawyers set the pace in pamphlets, petitions, town meetings, and provincial confrontation.
Longstanding conflicts between bench and bar become political grievances during the election season.
Legal qualifications and venal offices dominate the third-estate delegation because elections reward speaking, meeting, and drafting experience.
Legal training helps explain the deputies' prolonged caution before claiming authority outside established order procedure.

subjects.label: Electoral regulations of 24 January 1789
subjects.meaning: The royal regulations established constituencies, order assemblies, franchise rules, indirect voting, deputy ratios, and cahier production.
subjects.stance: The source presents the regulations as enabling extraordinary participation while also shaping outcomes through unequal social and institutional filters.

target_labels: Result of the King's Council of State, 27 December 1788

evidence.evidence_summary: The regulations define district groupings, exceptional provinces, order assemblies, suffrage, delegate stages, and the two-two-four allocation.
They require cahiers and structure a nationwide but socially filtered process.
The resulting delegation strongly favors legal professionals and officeholders.

subjects.label: Bailliages and senechaussees as constituencies
subjects.meaning: Ancient northern and southern judicial jurisdictions, sometimes grouped or supplemented, formed the principal national electoral geography.
subjects.stance: The chapter treats the districts as pragmatic inherited units whose exceptions mattered to representation.

evidence.evidence_summary: The Paris parlement's qualified retreat preserves the ancient judicial districts as the relevant 1614 feature.
The January rules group smaller districts, grant some towns separate representation, and add districts after petitions.
Judges from these courts later constitute a major segment of third-estate deputies.

subjects.label: Pays d'etats and electoral exceptions
subjects.meaning: Provinces with surviving or newly restored estates received different electoral treatment, especially Dauphine, Navarre, and Brittany.
subjects.stance: The author presents exceptions as politically contingent responses rather than a coherent federal principle.

evidence.evidence_summary: Dauphine and Navarre retain estate-based election, while Brittany's conflict produces separate arrangements for its orders.

subjects.label: Third-estate franchise and indirect election
subjects.meaning: Male taxpayers over twenty-five could enter primary assemblies, but delegates and final deputies were selected through successive indirect stages.
subjects.stance: The source balances the breadth of formal eligibility against the strong social narrowing produced by time, expense, and professional competence.

target_labels: Exclusion of peasants and artisans from final representation

evidence.evidence_summary: Formal primary eligibility is broad, but the third estate must elect delegates before ultimate deputies are chosen.
Indirect procedure allows widespread grievance participation while excluding those without leisure from deputy selection.
Even at the first stage many eligible voters abstain and favor socially similar representatives.
Costs and skill requirements help produce a delegation dominated by lawyers and officeholders.

subjects.label: Electoral participation and abstention
subjects.meaning: The elections drew unprecedented numbers into public affairs but turnout varied and was limited even in Paris.
subjects.stance: The chapter rejects both a simple democratic triumph narrative and a dismissal of the elections as socially closed.

target_labels: Exclusion of peasants and artisans from final representation

evidence.evidence_summary: Cahier drafting reaches communities across the country and creates unprecedented participation.
Only a minority exercises the primary vote in Paris, and participants tend to choose educated men like themselves.

subjects.label: Cahiers de doleances
subjects.meaning: Order and community grievance lists articulated expectations, directed deputies, and created an exceptional record of national political outlook.
subjects.stance: The author values their breadth while warning that local conflation and circulated models filtered out poorer concerns and reduced independence.

target_labels: Noble cahiers, fiscal equality, and voting compromises

evidence.evidence_summary: Every order assembly must prepare a grievance list alongside choosing deputies.
Village and corporate submissions are merged, often through patriotic models, producing unique national evidence while editing out poorer voices.
Clerical cahiers expose both lower-clergy reforms and enduring institutional commitments.
Noble cahiers show fiscal agreement but political fragmentation.

subjects.label: Elections of 1789 as democratic mobilization
subjects.meaning: The electoral and cahier process extended public deliberation across France on a scale unmatched in contemporary Europe.
subjects.stance: The chapter calls the spectacle extraordinarily democratic while preserving its indirect structure, unequal order rules, abstention, and social exclusions.

target_labels: Exclusion of peasants and artisans from final representation

evidence.evidence_summary: The drafting process draws the whole country into articulated grievances and aspirations and is judged unprecedented in Europe.
Election meetings nevertheless interact with economic rumor and popular disorder.
Order-specific electoral outcomes overturn established leadership in clergy and nobility.
The final social composition shows how mass participation narrowed into professional representation.

subjects.label: Government noninterference and structural influence on elections
subjects.meaning: Ministers largely avoided direct management of electoral outcomes, but the rules they issued reshaped representation in every order.
subjects.stance: The author distinguishes absence of overt manipulation from neutrality of institutional design.

evidence.evidence_summary: Necker declines serious interference, yet the rules empower parish priests, swamp former noble leaders, and eliminate poorer groups from final selection.
The resulting third-estate delegation reflects structural advantages for legally trained and officeholding participants.

subjects.label: Popular subsistence disorders during elections
subjects.meaning: Market riots, popular price setting, searches for hoarded grain, tax resistance, and attacks on property accompanied the election campaign.
subjects.stance: The source treats these disturbances as grounded in real scarcity and unemployment but not reducible to the constitutional programme of educated patriots.

target_labels: Marseilles patriotic guard and local governmental takeover

evidence.evidence_summary: Reports from many regions describe price fixing, searches for stored grain, and resistance to dues during the campaign.
The Reveillon crowd combines cheers for patriotic symbols with an attack on wealthy property.
Scarcity and rumor again combine with political crisis in the armed Paris rising.

subjects.label: Marseilles patriotic guard and local governmental takeover
subjects.meaning: Property-owning electors from all orders displaced ineffective city authorities and created a civic guard during March disorder.
subjects.stance: The event is treated as an early, initially shocking precursor to the municipal and militia transformations that followed July.

evidence.evidence_summary: Alarmed electors take over city government and form a substantial-citizen guard when established authorities cannot maintain order.

subjects.label: Reveillon riots
subjects.meaning: Misinterpreted wage remarks during Paris electoral meetings triggered rumor, attacks on manufacturers' property, and lethal repression.
subjects.stance: The author presents the episode as evidence that economic class tension could erupt inside a movement otherwise cheering the king, Necker, and the third estate.

target_labels: Public order and collapse of coercive authority

evidence.evidence_summary: A benevolent manufacturer's argument about affordable bread is recast as a wage-cut proposal, prompting crowds to sack homes and a factory.
The crowd's mixed patriotic and anti-rich slogans reveal tensions that unsettle arriving deputies.

subjects.label: Clerical deputies and parish-priest ascendancy
subjects.meaning: Electoral rules produced a first-estate delegation dominated by parish priests rather than bishops and corporate hierarchy.
subjects.stance: The chapter treats lower-clergy success as a real institutional defeat for hierarchy and a basis for later defections, while warning against assuming complete patriotic alignment.

evidence.evidence_summary: The electoral rules give parish clergy numerical weight over ecclesiastical corporations.
Three-quarters of clerical deputies are parish priests, and their cahiers demand stipends, access to office, and elected synods.
The clerical order narrowly accepts separate verification but refuses to constitute itself fully, seeking compromise.
Parish priests begin crossing to common verification.
Most remaining clergy join the National Assembly after royal enforcement fails.

subjects.label: Catholic Church's deeper institutional solidarity
subjects.meaning: Clergy across internal ranks shared commitments to stronger Church authority, education control, censorship, and limited Protestant toleration.
subjects.stance: The author cautions that excitement over parish-priest reform obscured solidarities more durable than the order's immediate representation dispute.

target_labels: Anti-clericalism in political and popular mobilization

evidence.evidence_summary: Clerical reform demands coexist with broad agreement on education, censorship, Catholic authority, and restricted Protestant rights.
The text stresses that this deeper unity outweighed disagreements about parish-priest status, though contemporaries largely missed it.

subjects.label: Noble deputies and electoral disarray
subjects.meaning: Noble elections displaced some expected leaders, produced conflicts among court, robe, provincial, and local elites, and yielded a fragmented delegation.
subjects.stance: The author rejects the image of a monolithic, confident nobility and emphasizes organizational weakness beneath wealth and status.

target_labels: Noble cahiers, fiscal equality, and voting compromises

evidence.evidence_summary: Electoral rules swamp court and sovereign-court elites with less experienced provincial nobles.
Courtiers and robe magistrates face strong electoral rejection by local noble assemblies.
Stormy assemblies, rival lists, and divergent cahiers reveal an order divided by old resentments.
The delegation's weakness and lack of unity contrast sharply with the third estate.

subjects.label: Noble cahiers, fiscal equality, and voting compromises
subjects.meaning: Noble grievance lists showed near unanimity on surrendering fiscal privilege but no comparable consensus on political voting or the basis of nobility.
subjects.stance: The chapter uses the cahiers to demonstrate genuine reform willingness alongside constitutional fragmentation.

evidence.evidence_summary: Noble cahiers broadly renounce tax privilege while dividing among order voting, head voting, and compromise arrangements.

subjects.label: Liberal nobles versus intransigent nobles
subjects.meaning: After election a reform minority sought accommodation with third-estate equality, while a larger bloc resisted common procedure.
subjects.stance: The author treats both camps as socially diverse and the division as political rather than a simple rich-poor split.

target_labels: Union of the three orders, 27 June 1789

evidence.evidence_summary: The text anticipates a liberal minority of roughly ninety opposed by an intransigent majority, with both drawn across noble society.
The noble order overwhelmingly completes separate verification.
A few noble allies remain separated while clergy begin defecting.
A minority crosses to the National Assembly before the king orders the full merger.

subjects.label: Breton nobility's election boycott
subjects.meaning: Breton nobles refused national election after losing the provincial-estates route and sent no deputies.
subjects.stance: The boycott is a significant consequence of the province's constitutional crisis, not representative of all noble electoral behavior.

evidence.evidence_summary: The Breton nobility boycotts the election because its delegation will not be returned through the provincial estates.

subjects.label: Social composition of third-estate deputies
subjects.meaning: The final third-estate contingent was socially and professionally homogeneous, dominated by lawyers and officeholders rather than producers or laborers.
subjects.stance: The author treats this composition as the outcome of electoral filters and relevant skills, not as proof that the third estate at large shared the deputies' social position.
acceptable_access: lawyers and officeholders in the third estate

target_labels: Government noninterference and structural influence on elections
Exclusion of peasants and artisans from final representation

evidence.evidence_summary: The indirect system removes those without leisure before final selection.
Primary voters favor educated men like themselves and final deputies must meet expenses.
Legal qualifications and venal offices overwhelmingly outnumber deputies from trade or industry.

subjects.label: Exclusion of peasants and artisans from final representation
subjects.meaning: Peasants and artisans could enter some primary assemblies but did not survive the indirect process into the final delegation.
subjects.stance: The chapter distinguishes formal primary inclusion from effective exclusion at the stage where deputies were selected.

evidence.evidence_summary: Indirect voting and lack of leisure remove peasants, artisans, and many poorer citizens before deputy selection.
No peasants or artisans pass beyond the first stage, and even eligible Paris voters participate selectively.

subjects.label: Third-estate political unity
subjects.meaning: Shared legal-cultural background and commitments to head voting plus civil and fiscal equality made third-estate deputies unusually cohesive.
subjects.stance: The source contrasts their unity with the other orders while avoiding the claim that all deputies arrived nationally famous or socially representative.

target_labels: Declaration of the National Assembly, 17 June

evidence.evidence_summary: Most third-estate deputies are locally known rather than national leaders, but shared background and equality commitments unite them.
They refuse separate verification because it would preserve order voting.
A large majority backs Sieyes's final appeal and unilateral roll-call.
The Assembly title and tax resolution turn cohesion into a claim of sovereignty.

subjects.label: Opening of the Estates-General, 5 May 1789
subjects.meaning: The ceremonial opening displayed the three orders' traditional distinctions but failed to address the voting crisis.
subjects.stance: The author emphasizes disappointed expectation and the political cost of speeches that seemed evasive and overfocused on finance.

evidence.evidence_summary: Elaborate processions display corporate order distinctions before huge crowds, while the opening addresses disappoint.
Failure to settle voting makes verification the first decisive struggle.

subjects.label: Necker's equivocation at the opening
subjects.meaning: Necker recommended common voting for some questions but defended possible order voting for others and left change to voluntary agreement.
subjects.stance: The chapter treats his position as an attempt at conciliation that instead strengthened determination to decide verification before all other business.

target_labels: Necker's return, popularity, and political role

evidence.evidence_summary: The opening speech concentrates on finance and promises reform without confronting the order question.
Selective common voting and separate preliminary verification leave all sides dissatisfied and make procedure decisive.

subjects.label: Verification of powers
subjects.meaning: Validation of deputies' credentials became the procedural mechanism for choosing between three constituted orders and one national body.
subjects.stance: The author presents verification as substantively constitutional, not a technical pretext, because separate validation implied separate voting.

target_labels: Vote by head versus vote by order
Sieyes's final appeal and roll-call, 10-12 June
Declaration of the National Assembly, 17 June

evidence.evidence_summary: The third refuses separate verification while nobility completes it and clergy narrowly begins it.
Failed negotiations and royal inaction lead the Commons toward unilateral common roll-call.
Clerical participation in the roll-call gives the process a claim beyond the third estate.
Completed common verification supports adoption of the National Assembly title.

subjects.label: The third estate's adoption of 'the Commons'
subjects.meaning: The third estate styled itself the Commons while refusing to constitute separately.
subjects.stance: The title expressed an expanding representative claim but remained short of the explicit national sovereignty later asserted.

target_labels: Declaration of the National Assembly, 17 June
Third estate as nation and semantic shift in patriotism

evidence.evidence_summary: Deputies adopt the tendentious Commons label during their stand against separate verification.
Talk of unilateral national action grows as the Commons organizes itself and sends a final appeal.

subjects.label: Clergy's divided response and defections
subjects.meaning: The first estate combined narrow procedural votes for separation with sustained hesitation, conscience-based conciliation, and growing defections to common verification.
subjects.stance: The chapter treats lower-clergy crossings as decisive but gradual, reflecting both institutional solidarity and pressure from public events.
acceptable_access: clerical defections to the third estate

target_labels: Union of the three orders, 27 June 1789

evidence.evidence_summary: Clergy narrowly votes for separate verification but declines to declare itself constituted and seeks compromise.
Conscience, political stalemate, and news of popular distress increase pressure on parish priests.
Nineteen clerics begin crossing during common roll-call.
A narrow clerical majority votes to join immediately before the Tennis Court Oath.
Most remaining clergy cross after royal coercion fails.

subjects.label: Sieyes's final appeal and roll-call, 10-12 June
subjects.meaning: Sieyes moved a last invitation to the other orders followed by unilateral verification if they refused.
subjects.stance: The author identifies the ensuing roll-call as the start of the true revolutionary struggle because deputies knowingly took national legality into their own hands.

target_labels: Revolutionary legality and the law-soaked third estate
Declaration of the National Assembly, 17 June

evidence.evidence_summary: The Commons overwhelmingly approves a final appeal and begins verification without the other orders when no answer arrives.
Clerical defections during the roll-call broaden the verified body and create the naming problem that follows.

subjects.label: Revolutionary legality and the law-soaked third estate
subjects.meaning: Legally trained deputies delayed breaking precedent, recognized the irrevocability of unilateral action, and used formal verification and resolutions to construct new authority.
subjects.stance: The author presents the rupture as deliberate and reluctant rather than spontaneous lawlessness.

target_labels: Declaration of the National Assembly, 17 June
National Assembly's tax resolution and sovereignty claim

evidence.evidence_summary: The long wait before unilateral roll-call demonstrates reluctance to sever legal continuity and awareness that return was impossible.
Deputies debate exact names for the verified national body instead of simply declaring an undefined revolution.
The Assembly couples its new title to a carefully framed provisional tax authorization.
After royal nullification, deputies renew prior acts and assert personal inviolability through formal resolutions.

subjects.label: Spectators, crowds, and public pressure at Versailles
subjects.meaning: Open galleries and increasingly numerous visitors rewarded uncompromising speeches, intimidated moderates, and made popular backing visible to deputies and the crown.
subjects.stance: The chapter treats spectators as a real political force without claiming that crowd approval alone determined every decision.

target_labels: Popular intervention in the constitutional revolution
Declaration of the National Assembly, 17 June
National Assembly's defiance of the king

evidence.evidence_summary: Open galleries applaud intransigence and drown out caution as unilateral verification begins.
Public impatience presses the naming debate toward the National Assembly.
Crowds surround the Tennis Court and turn continued meeting into a public act of resistance.
Versailles crowds penetrate the palace and threaten opponents after the Royal Session.

subjects.label: Political journalism and daily reporting
subjects.meaning: Fast, partisan reporting connected proceedings at Versailles to a national public and sustained pressure during the verification crisis.
subjects.stance: The source credits journalism with widening participation while noting the bias of even accurate accounts.

target_labels: Spectators, crowds, and public pressure at Versailles
Mirabeau's leadership and Letters to His Constituents

evidence.evidence_summary: Daily reports carry the Estates' stalemate to an already mobilized public.
Mirabeau's regular letters marshal subscribers behind the patriotic interpretation of events.

subjects.label: Mirabeau's leadership and Letters to His Constituents
subjects.meaning: Mirabeau emerged from distrust to become a powerful orator and journalist able to articulate the deputies' developing national claims.
subjects.stance: The author recognizes his accuracy and political insight while expressly qualifying his reports as partisan.

target_labels: National Assembly's defiance of the king
Palais Royal as a forcing-house of opinion

evidence.evidence_summary: Mirabeau is one of very few outsiders elected by the third estate under Necker's cross-order rule.
His letters give the public regular, detailed, and politically slanted accounts of proceedings.
His oratory expresses positions other deputies have not yet fully formulated.
His refusal to yield without force becomes the clearest expression of Assembly defiance.
He moves the unopposed petition to remove troops from the Paris region.

subjects.label: Palais Royal as a forcing-house of opinion
subjects.meaning: The Palais Royal served as a dense market for pamphlets, rumor, debate, oratory, and rapid crowd mobilization.
subjects.stance: The chapter treats it as a central urban infrastructure of political opinion rather than merely a meeting place.

evidence.evidence_summary: Publication stalls, coffeehouses, and improvised speakers make the complex the capital's most intense arena of political debate.
Rumor that Necker has resigned produces immediate mass agitation there.
Mutinous guards are publicly celebrated through Palais-Royal collections.
News of Necker's dismissal reaches the site and triggers mourning, crowd movement, and a citywide trial of strength.

subjects.label: Declaration of the National Assembly, 17 June
subjects.meaning: The verified representatives adopted a national title and ceased to define themselves as one corporate order.
subjects.stance: The author treats the declaration as the institutional conversion of representation into sovereignty, not a merely verbal change.

target_labels: Sieyes's final appeal and roll-call, 10-12 June
National Assembly's tax resolution and sovereignty claim

evidence.evidence_summary: Clerical participation and common verification force deputies to decide whom the body represents.
An overwhelming vote adopts the National Assembly name and immediately supports a sovereign fiscal resolution.
The Royal Session attempts to annul the declaration, but deputies formally renew it.
By mid-July the Estates-General has been replaced by a single sovereign national body.

subjects.label: National Assembly's tax resolution and sovereignty claim
subjects.meaning: The Assembly declared existing taxes unlawful yet provisionally valid while it continued to sit.
subjects.stance: The author treats the resolution as an unmistakable sovereign claim because dissolution would authorize fiscal disobedience.

target_labels: Declaration of the National Assembly, 17 June

evidence.evidence_summary: The Assembly unanimously conditions continued tax authorization on its own survival, directly challenging independent royal fiscal authority.

subjects.label: Court party, queen, and Artois
subjects.meaning: The queen, Artois, and allied courtiers pressed for strong measures, altered conciliation plans, supported troop concentrations, and sought Necker's removal.
subjects.stance: The chapter presents them as a persistent counter-revolutionary pressure within government but not as masters of a coherent or enforceable strategy.

target_labels: Royal Session planning and locked meeting hall
Marie Antoinette's role in the Court response
Count d'Artois and the strong-measures party

evidence.evidence_summary: Rumors identify the queen and Artois with efforts to remove Necker before the Estates meet.
Their party modifies Necker's Royal Session proposals and supports troop reinforcement.
They continue seeking Necker's removal and more pliable ministers while forces concentrate.
The Court coterie's attempt to reverse June fails when popular pressure and unreliable troops strip the crown of coercive power.

subjects.label: Royal Session planning and locked meeting hall
subjects.meaning: Secretive preparation for a royal intervention left deputies facing locked doors and soldiers on 20 June.
subjects.stance: The chapter emphasizes that poor notification and coercive appearances converted even opponents of 17 June into defenders of the Assembly's right to meet.

evidence.evidence_summary: Court revisions, troop reinforcement, and unannounced closure make dissolution appear imminent and produce principled resistance.

subjects.label: Tennis Court Oath
subjects.meaning: Deputies pledged not to disperse until a constitution and public regeneration were secured.
subjects.stance: The oath is presented as a deliberate collective response to apparent royal obstruction that bound the Assembly to a constituent mission.

target_labels: Royal Session planning and locked meeting hall
National Assembly's defiance of the king
Declaration of the National Assembly, 17 June

evidence.evidence_summary: Locked out of their hall, deputies relocate and swear to remain assembled until constitutional regeneration is achieved.
After the king orders separation, the Assembly renews the oath and its prior resolutions.

subjects.label: Royal Session of 23 June
subjects.meaning: The king offered major reforms while nullifying Assembly acts, preserving corporate orders and privilege vetoes, excluding spectators, and commanding separate deliberation.
subjects.stance: The author judges the programme imaginative and potentially effective if earlier, but fatally compromised by timing, coercive form, and retained order privilege.

target_labels: Declaration of the National Assembly, 17 June
National Assembly's defiance of the king
Collapse of Louis XVI's strategy and royal decision-making

evidence.evidence_summary: The king combines fiscal, administrative, and civil reforms with annulment of 17 June, order vetoes, closed sessions, and an enforcement threat.
Deputy refusal and the king's immediate abandonment of coercion destroy the strategy.

subjects.label: Louis XVI's reform programme of 23 June
subjects.meaning: The royal declaration promised consent-based taxation, relief from arbitrary imprisonment, tax and labor reform, serfdom abolition, and provincial estates.
subjects.stance: The author stresses that substantial reforms arrived too late and were undercut by inviolable feudal property, voluntary privilege surrender, order vetoes, and royal supremacy.

target_labels: National Assembly's tax resolution and sovereignty claim

evidence.evidence_summary: The programme combines forward-looking reforms with protections for feudal and corporate privilege and an assertion that Assembly acts require royal approval.

subjects.label: National Assembly's defiance of the king
subjects.meaning: The Assembly refused the command to disperse, renewed its acts and oath, and declared members inviolable.
subjects.stance: The author presents the stand as decisive because the crown's failure to enforce its order transformed asserted sovereignty into effective power.

target_labels: Collapse of Louis XVI's strategy and royal decision-making
Union of the three orders, 27 June 1789

evidence.evidence_summary: Deputies remain after other orders leave, reject ceremonial commands, and formally reaffirm their national acts.
The king permits them to stay, popular support expands, and clergy and nobles begin joining in greater numbers.

subjects.label: Collapse of Louis XVI's strategy and royal decision-making
subjects.meaning: Grief, delay, divided counsel, and sudden abandonment of enforcement repeatedly nullified royal and ministerial plans.
subjects.stance: The source explains failure through political incapacity and lack of reliable force rather than presenting every royal retreat as voluntary benevolence.

target_labels: Louis XVI and the collapse of royal authority
Union of the three orders, 27 June 1789

evidence.evidence_summary: The dauphin's death contributes to royal and ministerial paralysis during the verification crisis.
The king underestimates the National Assembly label while ministers disagree over response.
A casual permission for deputies to remain throws away the Royal Session strategy.
The king later withdraws troops because commanders cannot assure obedience.
The monarchy no longer has the capacity to reverse the Assembly's claims.

subjects.label: Necker's resignation crisis of 23 June
subjects.meaning: Necker's absence from the Royal Session and attempted resignation revealed division inside government and inflamed popular fears.
subjects.stance: The source distinguishes Necker's personal popularity from the more consequential constitutional content that crowds often overlooked.

target_labels: Necker's return, popularity, and political role
Popular intervention in the constitutional revolution

evidence.evidence_summary: Necker stays away because Court changes compromise his conciliation plan and offers his resignation.
Rumor of dismissal ignites the Palais Royal and crowds focus on his status more than the king's constitutional proposals.

subjects.label: French Guards' politicization and mutiny
subjects.meaning: The French Guards moved from repressing Paris crowds to refusing public-order duties, deserting, and supplying military expertise to the uprising.
subjects.stance: The chapter treats this change as crucial to the crown's loss of reliable coercion and to the Bastille's surrender.

target_labels: Storming and surrender of the Bastille

evidence.evidence_summary: The regiment fires on the Reveillon crowd in April.
Companies refuse public-order duty after the Royal Session crisis.
Mutinous guards are freed and publicly celebrated while troop concentrations grow.
Defecting guards bring cannon and expertise to the Bastille, while their example undermines confidence in other regiments.

subjects.label: Union of the three orders, 27 June 1789
subjects.meaning: Clerical and noble defections, popular pressure, and failed royal coercion compelled the formal merger of the remaining orders into the National Assembly.
subjects.stance: The author treats union as a victory for national representation but not the end of popular or Court conflict.

target_labels: National Assembly's defiance of the king

evidence.evidence_summary: Initial clerical defections erode the first estate's solidarity.
A clerical majority votes to join immediately before the locked-hall confrontation.
Most clergy and dozens of nobles cross before the king orders the remaining orders to unite.
Deputies briefly believe the constitutional struggle has ended, although popular ferment and Court suspicion persist.

subjects.label: Popular intervention in the constitutional revolution
subjects.meaning: Petitions, demonstrations, galleries, crowds, militias, troop fraternization, and armed action repeatedly altered elite choices and protected the National Assembly.
subjects.stance: The chapter makes popular participation causally indispensable while distinguishing organized opinion, subsistence protest, property-owning militias, and uncontrolled violence.

target_labels: Union of the three orders, 27 June 1789
Spectators, crowds, and public pressure at Versailles

evidence.evidence_summary: Nationwide meetings and petitions overwhelm the agenda of the Notables.
Provincial mobilization turns order conflict into violent confrontation.
Public galleries and daily reports exert pressure during the legal rupture.
Crowds and wavering troops make royal enforcement against the Assembly unreliable.
Paris organizes and arms after Necker's dismissal.
Armed civilians and defecting guards seize the Bastille and compel withdrawal of troops.
Popular support defeats the Court effort and convinces Parisians they saved national liberty.

subjects.label: Court troop build-up around Paris
subjects.meaning: Late-June and early-July reinforcement concentrated more than twenty thousand troops, including foreign regiments, around Paris.
subjects.stance: The author judges intimidation and reversal of June concessions to be the true purpose, rejecting the official public-order explanation.

target_labels: Storming and surrender of the Bastille

evidence.evidence_summary: A rapid fivefold troop increase under Broglie's command appears designed to intimidate Paris and undo concessions.
Cavalry action and reports of military preparation convince Parisians that the feared offensive has begun.
The force is numerically sufficient but cannot be used confidently because troop loyalty has eroded.

subjects.label: Dismissal of Necker, 11 July 1789
subjects.meaning: Removal of the minister identified with conciliation, grain controls, and public trust signaled an attempted Court reversal.
subjects.stance: The dismissal is treated as the immediate political trigger of the Paris uprising, acting upon existing troop fear and subsistence crisis.

target_labels: Attacks on Paris toll gates and customs wall
Storming and surrender of the Bastille

evidence.evidence_summary: The Court removes Necker and other ministers and installs Broglie and Breteuil while troops surround Paris.
News at the Palais Royal turns anxiety into mourning, crowd action, and a search for arms.
The attempted reversal collapses before the new ministry can implement a clear programme.

subjects.label: Grain-trade debate in the National Assembly
subjects.meaning: Deputies debated grain freedom during peak scarcity but avoided a decisive position.
subjects.stance: The episode shows ideological preference for free trade constrained by awareness that public conditions made advocacy politically dangerous.

evidence.evidence_summary: The Assembly debates grain policy for several days without resolution as riots and near-record Paris prices make frank free-trade advocacy hazardous.

subjects.label: Paris electors and citizens' militia
subjects.meaning: Paris electors continued meeting after elections and created an armed civic force when royal troops and police could not be trusted.
subjects.stance: The source presents the militia as a property-protecting response to both despotism and popular violence, initially too weak to control the uprising.

target_labels: Public order and collapse of coercive authority
Marseilles patriotic guard and local governmental takeover
Popular intervention in the constitutional revolution

evidence.evidence_summary: Electors activate a citizens' militia and patrols as armed crowds outpace established authority.
Electors attempt negotiation at the Bastille before the crowd and defecting guards determine the outcome.

subjects.label: Attacks on Paris toll gates and customs wall
subjects.meaning: Armed crowds destroyed tax barriers and sections of the customs wall after Necker's dismissal.
subjects.stance: The attacks link subsistence anger, fiscal resentment, and political revolt rather than serving as mere background vandalism.

evidence.evidence_summary: Crowds follow the Lyon example by burning gatehouses and breaching the wall during the first night of armed revolt.

subjects.label: Saint-Lazare grain search and anti-clerical violence
subjects.meaning: Armed crowds looted the monastery after finding stored grain during a search for weapons and suspected hoarding.
subjects.stance: The incident is treated as a revealing convergence of subsistence fear, sacrilege, and anti-clerical suspicion, not a central institutional campaign.

target_labels: Anti-clericalism in political and popular mobilization

evidence.evidence_summary: Discovery of grain during an arms search confirms crowd suspicions and leads to looting with anti-clerical overtones.

subjects.label: Seizure of arms at the Invalides
subjects.meaning: Paris crowds acquired muskets and cannon from the veterans' hospital before moving on the Bastille.
subjects.stance: The episode matters as the material step that made the supposedly formidable fortress vulnerable to trained attackers.

target_labels: Storming and surrender of the Bastille

evidence.evidence_summary: Crowds remove small arms and cannon from the Invalides and transport them toward the city center and Bastille.

subjects.label: Storming and surrender of the Bastille
subjects.meaning: Armed crowds, failed negotiation, garrison fire, French Guards' expertise, and cannon pressure produced the fortress's surrender.
subjects.stance: The author explains the event materially and politically, treating it as the climax that broke royal coercion rather than as an inexplicable symbolic eruption.

target_labels: Seizure of arms at the Invalides
Parisians as guardians of revolutionary liberty

evidence.evidence_summary: Negotiation collapses after garrison fire; defecting guards bring cannon and force surrender of the poorly defended fortress.
The author identifies the Bastille as the climax of the popular movement that defeated the Court's counteraction.

subjects.label: Army unreliability and Broglie's advice
subjects.meaning: Mutiny, desertion, low morale, civilian appeals, and commanders' caution made the army an unsafe instrument against Paris.
subjects.stance: The source explicitly rejects lack of troop numbers as the reason for retreat; the decisive limitation was doubtful obedience and the risk of wider defection.

evidence.evidence_summary: Broglie concludes that sufficient forces cannot safely be ordered into mass repression because loyalty and morale are uncertain.

subjects.label: Withdrawal of royal troops
subjects.meaning: Louis XVI ordered the forces around Paris to disperse after the Bastille and advice that the army could not be relied upon.
subjects.stance: The author denies that natural royal benevolence explains the retreat; it was compelled by lost coercive capacity.

target_labels: Storming and surrender of the Bastille

evidence.evidence_summary: The king reverses his military policy after commanders warn that repression may provoke defection and carnage.
Withdrawal forces acceptance of the National Assembly's acts and ends the attempted Court reversal.

subjects.label: End of royal authority
subjects.meaning: The monarchy retained formal status but no longer possessed the enforceable power to impose its will or undo the National Assembly.
subjects.stance: The chapter treats the loss of coercive authority as the decisive constitutional result of July, not merely a temporary ministerial defeat.

target_labels: National Assembly's defiance of the king

evidence.evidence_summary: The king's acceptance of military unreliability acknowledges that he cannot enforce his will.
The Estates-General has disappeared into a sovereign National Assembly and the Court cannot reverse the change.

subjects.label: Parisians as guardians of revolutionary liberty
subjects.meaning: Victory over the Court convinced the people of Paris that they had saved the National Assembly and acquired a continuing protective role.
subjects.stance: The source treats this self-conception as a durable political consequence of the Bastille, without endorsing every act of crowd violence.
acceptable_access: people of Paris and National Assembly

target_labels: Storming and surrender of the Bastille
Popular intervention in the constitutional revolution

evidence.evidence_summary: The chapter concludes that Parisians believed their intervention alone preserved the Assembly and the liberty it represented.

subjects.label: From revolt to Revolution
subjects.meaning: The combined collapse of royal coercion, creation of a sovereign National Assembly, and popular defeat of counteraction constituted a qualitative revolutionary break.
subjects.stance: The author's conclusion is firm even while the famous reported exchange used to dramatize it may be apocryphal.

target_labels: Storming and surrender of the Bastille
Declaration of the National Assembly, 17 June

evidence.evidence_summary: The final synthesis identifies national sovereignty, defeated royal authority, and popular guardianship as a Revolution rather than a normal disturbance.

subjects.label: Louis XVI and the collapse of royal authority
subjects.meaning: Louis XVI moved from cautious constitutional management through failed coercive interventions to recognition that he could not enforce his will.
subjects.stance: The author rejects both a benevolent-monarch explanation and a single-villain account, emphasizing indecision, divided counsel, misjudged timing, and loss of reliable force.

target_labels: Collapse of Louis XVI's strategy and royal decision-making

evidence.evidence_summary: The king rejects privileged petitions and hints that national representation is a matter between monarch and nation.
He accepts Necker's compromise that doubles the third while deferring common voting.
Personal grief and inertia contribute to ministerial paralysis during the verification crisis.
The Royal Session asserts approval power and orders separate deliberation while offering reforms.
Permission for defiant deputies to remain collapses the enforcement plan.
Military unreliability forces withdrawal of troops.
The king can no longer reverse the sovereign National Assembly and royal authority is effectively ended.

subjects.label: Marie Antoinette's role in the Court response
subjects.meaning: The queen supported strong measures, troop reinforcement, revisions to Necker's Royal Session plan, and continued efforts to remove him.
subjects.stance: The chapter treats her as an influential member of the Court party, not as the sole designer or controller of counteraction.

target_labels: Royal Session planning and locked meeting hall

evidence.evidence_summary: The queen's party supports military reinforcement and alters Necker's conciliation proposals.
She remains committed to removing Necker and reversing the June concessions.
The Court coterie fails when popular support and troop unreliability defeat coercion.

subjects.label: Count d'Artois and the strong-measures party
subjects.meaning: Artois repeatedly pressed for Necker's removal and forceful resistance to third-estate and Assembly claims.
subjects.stance: The source identifies him as a sustained Court-party actor while leaving the exact post-dismissal ministerial programme uncertain.

evidence.evidence_summary: Court rumors identify Artois with pressure for Necker's dismissal before the Estates open.
He welcomes troop reinforcement and supports a coercive Court response to Assembly sovereignty.
His party secures Necker's removal and replacement by harder-line ministers.
The attempted reversal associated with the Court party is defeated by the July movement.

subjects.label: Adrien Duport
subjects.meaning: Duport served as organizer and institutional bridge among radical magistrates, elite reform networks, publicity, and later elected deputies.
subjects.stance: The chapter treats his influence as catalytic but insufficient to control the national movement he helped focus.

target_labels: Restoration and decline of the parlements

evidence.evidence_summary: Duport hosts and helps lead the elite reform society that finances anti-1614 mobilization.
He participates in the successful parliamentary lobbying that qualifies the court's September declaration.
He is elected among the small surviving group of celebrated robe magistrates.

subjects.label: Mounier
subjects.meaning: Mounier helped formulate the Dauphine representative model and brought unusually extensive provincial political experience into the Estates-General.
subjects.stance: The text treats him as an important reform leader without making his programme identical to every later radical step.

evidence.evidence_summary: Mounier helps lead the Grenoble movement that produces the Vizille settlement.
He is one of the few third-estate patriot leaders known nationally before the wider campaign.
He enters the Estates as a recognized Dauphine leader among many unknown deputies.

subjects.label: Barnave
subjects.meaning: Barnave emerged from the Dauphine movement as a nationally recognized advocate and elected third-estate deputy.
subjects.stance: The chapter presents him as part of the province's influential leadership rather than as an isolated celebrity.

evidence.evidence_summary: Barnave joins Mounier in prompting the cross-order provincial assembly and its representative principles.
He is named among the earliest nationally known third-estate leaders.
He exemplifies the legally trained deputies elected to the third estate.

subjects.label: Bailly
subjects.meaning: Bailly combined scientific reputation with third-estate election and early procedural leadership as president of the Commons.
subjects.stance: The source gives him a defined institutional role but does not yet analyze the later mayoral career that begins outside this chunk.

target_labels: The third estate's adoption of 'the Commons'

evidence.evidence_summary: The astronomer is one of the nationally prominent figures in an otherwise locally known third-estate contingent.
The Commons elects him president as it establishes procedures and prepares unilateral action.

subjects.label: Duke d'Orleans
subjects.meaning: Orleans sought popular acclaim in the Notables, gained election among noble deputies, provided the Palais Royal arena, and joined pressure for common verification.
subjects.stance: The chapter presents him as a recurrent facilitator and participant, without attributing the entire popular movement to an Orleanist plot.

target_labels: Palais Royal as a forcing-house of opinion

evidence.evidence_summary: Orleans helps press the Notables to reject the 1614 forms.
He secures election among the noble deputies.
His Palais Royal property supplies the capital's central space for publication, rumor, and oratory.
He leads a minority seeking common verification before crossing nobles join the National Assembly.

subjects.label: Robespierre's entry into politics
subjects.meaning: Robespierre first gained wider notice through an appeal against Artois's privileged provincial structure and was then elected as an advocate.
subjects.stance: The treatment establishes an early political entry point but does not yet sustain a separate account of his mature programme.

evidence.evidence_summary: His published appeal urges Artois to abandon its archaic privileged estates.
He appears among the advocates elected to the third estate.

subjects.label: Fiscal equality and tax privilege
subjects.meaning: Renunciation of order-based tax exemptions commanded broader agreement than political equality or common voting.
subjects.stance: The chapter repeatedly distinguishes fiscal equality from surrender of political, social, feudal, and corporate privilege.

target_labels: Privilege as a political and social concept
Vote by head versus vote by order
National Assembly's tax resolution and sovereignty claim

evidence.evidence_summary: Notables reaffirm fiscal equality while rejecting representative reform, and the public finds the distinction inadequate.
Princes offer fiscal equality as the limit of legitimate third-estate aspiration.
Sieyes rejects noble assurances that fiscal surrender exhausts privilege.
Clergy expect institutional gains in return for giving up fiscal exemptions.
